planting.note: Cultivation is not possible — ghost pipe has no chlorophyll and survives entirely by tapping into mycorrhizal fungi that are themselves connected to living tree roots; digging or transplanting severs this connection and kills the plant.

directions: Ghost pipe is a translucent white, waxy-stemmed perennial that lacks chlorophyll entirely and survives by tapping into mycorrhizal fungi that are themselves linked to the roots of nearby hardwood trees, making it a true parasite of a fungal network rather than a conventional green plant. A single nodding, bell-like flower tops each stem from midsummer into early fall in the deep leaf litter of mixed deciduous and evergreen New England forests, gradually turning upright and blackening as the seed capsule matures. It offers little to pollinators beyond occasional bumblebee visits and cannot be propagated or transplanted by any gardener. Treat a sighting as a sign of healthy, undisturbed forest soil and leave the plant exactly where it is found.

planting.note: Cannot be cultivated or transplanted; it attaches to living oak roots through haustoria and depends completely on an intact, mature host root system that cannot be recreated in a garden.

directions: American bear-corn emerges each spring as a cluster of thick, scaly, tan-to-yellow stalks that push up through leaf litter at the base of mature oaks, resembling small clusters of corn cobs rather than anything typically recognized as a wildflower. Lacking leaves and chlorophyll, it draws all of its water and nutrients directly from oak roots through specialized haustorial connections, and small cream-colored tubular flowers open along the stalk in late spring, visited mainly by bumblebees before the plant withers back underground by midsummer. It turns up through New England's oak-dominated deciduous forests and depends entirely on a living, established oak, so it cannot be propagated or grown apart from its host tree. The plant is best treated as an indicator of mature, undisturbed oak forest rather than a candidate for any garden.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into consistently saturated, mineral-rich, cool soil in partial shade; this fen specialist will not tolerate drying out and is best suited to a constructed bog garden or streamside seep rather than an ordinary perennial bed.

directions: Bog Jacob's-ladder produces loose, nodding clusters of blue-violet, bell-shaped flowers with conspicuously protruding stamens from early to midsummer atop stems lined with ladder-like compound leaves, and the blossoms are an important nectar source for long-tongued bumblebees able to reach deep into the narrow corolla. Within New England the species survives only in a handful of calcareous fens, forested wetland margins, and cool streambanks in Maine and Vermont, where it is formally ranked as critically rare, with scattered additional populations continuing south through the Appalachians. Because it is adapted to constantly saturated, mineral-rich, cold seep water, garden success depends on replicating a fen or bog-edge environment rather than typical perennial border conditions. Only propagate from responsibly nursery-grown divisions given the species' rarity — never collect from wild stands.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic, peaty soil in partial shade; mountain holly is dioecious, so both a male and a female plant are needed for berry production.

directions: Mountain holly, long known by its older name Nemopanthus mucronatus before taxonomists folded the genus into Ilex, is a deciduous shrub of cold northern wetlands that bears small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers on slender stalks in late spring, followed by bright red berry-like drupes that ripen through summer and persist on female plants into fall. The modest flowers draw small native bees, while the fruit is an important late-season food for migrating songbirds and is a larval host for the striking Columbia silkmoth found in northern Maine. It grows naturally in boreal bogs, swamp margins, lakeshores, and cool subalpine forest openings throughout New England, especially at higher elevations and further north, and performs best in consistently moist to wet, acidic ground. Because both sexes are needed to fruit and it strongly prefers boggy or seasonally flooded soil, it suits a native wetland or rain-garden planting rather than an average shrub border.

planting.note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial shade; round-leaved dogwood tolerates thin, rocky soils on ledges and slopes better than most dogwoods but also thrives on richer forest-edge sites.

directions: Round-leaved dogwood, also classified in some references as Cornus rugosa, is named for its broad, nearly circular, velvety leaves that set it apart from other native dogwoods at a glance, and it bears flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring to early summer that draw a wide range of native bees and other pollinating insects. The flowers give way to pale blue, berry-like drupes by late summer that are quickly taken by thrushes, vireos, and other woodland birds, making it a valuable understory wildlife shrub. It turns up scattered through the forests, ledges, talus slopes, and forest edges of New England and the Adirondacks, often on rocky or thin soils where other shrubs struggle, and tends to spread into openings by root suckering over time. Give it partial shade and well-drained soil, and allow room for it to form a loose, multi-stemmed thicket rather than training it as a single-trunk specimen.
